docs.title: 1. What?
docs.text: A persistent audit record documenting major decisions made during the project lifecycle.

docs.title: 2. Why?
docs.text: Prevents relitigating settled decisions and provides clear traceability for project direction and governance.

docs.title: 3. When?
docs.text: Maintained continuously from kickoff through final delivery.

docs.title: 4. Who?
docs.text: Documented by the Project Manager in consultation with technical leads and business decision makers.

docs.title: Tailoring Tips
docs.text:
• Include trade-offs and rejected alternatives to explain why the decision was taken.
  • Link decisions directly to change requests or risk register mitigations.

docs.title: 5. How?
docs.text:
To accurately and professionally complete the Decision Log, the responsible party must populate the following critical sections based on the project context (ensure parameters.md is referenced for global project variables):

  • ID: Unique identifier for the decision (e.g., DEC-01).

  • Responsible Party: The person or entity responsible for making and enforcing the decision.
  • Date: The date on which the decision was officially agreed or approved.

docs.title: 1. What?

docs.title: Project Artifact: Retrospective
docs.text:
Document Reference: PMO-05.08

This document provides a comprehensive, professional reference to understand the purpose and effective usage of the Retrospective in alignment with the Tasleemat framework.

docs.title: 1. What?
docs.text:
A formal Tasleemat-aligned project document known as the Retrospective, an activity performed at the end of every sprint. The information is usually recorded on sticky notes or in software. A common approach is called a starfish and collects Start, Stop, Keep, More, and Less. The intent is to improve the performance of the team and make them more efficient in each subsequent sprint.

It records the session context, the five starfish observations, the action items taken from them with an owner and a review date, and the outcome of those actions at the next retrospective. The FLAP alternative is carried as a removable section.

docs.title: 2. Why?
docs.text: Because a retrospective that records what happened without recording what will change is a meeting rather than a feedback loop. The outcome column is what turns a list of good intentions into a change in how the team works, and without it the same actions are carried forward sprint after sprint.

docs.title: 3. When?
docs.text: This artifact is prepared at the EXECUTING Process Group, at the end of every sprint, or at whatever interval the team has agreed, which the form records explicitly.

docs.title: 4. Who?
docs.text: Responsibilities: Facilitated by the Team Lead with the whole team present, including anyone who will be affected by the actions. Outcomes are reviewed by the Project Manager at the following retrospective.

docs.title: Tailoring Tips
docs.text:
• Instead of a starfish approach you can use "FLAP," which stands for Future Considerations, Lessons, Accomplishments, and Problems. Use one or the other, not both: two parallel forms each get half-filled and neither is trusted.
  • You can colour code information to indicate a category, such as technical, process, people, environment, etc. This makes a pattern visible that a list of sentences hides.
  • Add or remove rows as needed. Some teams run the retrospective per sprint, others per release, and the template should say which.
  • Keep one item per row and to a single sentence. An item that needs explaining is two items, or it is not yet understood well enough to act on.

docs.title: 1. Pre-requisites & Inputs (Upstream Dependencies)
docs.text:
• Mandatory:
    • Project Management Plan (PMO-04.01.01)
    • Approved Baselines (Scope/Schedule/Cost)
  • Optional / Contextual:
    • Risk Register (PMO-04.08.02)
    • Stakeholder Engagement Plan (PMO-04.10.01)

docs.title: 2. Downstream Dependents
docs.text:
• Mandatory:
    • Project Status Reports (PMO-06.01)
    • Change Log (PMO-05.04)
    • Lessons Learned Summary (PMO-07.01)
  • Optional / Contextual:
    • Variance Analysis (PMO-06.04)
    • Decision Log (PMO-05.02)

docs.title: 5. How?
docs.text:
To accurately and professionally complete the RETROSPECTIVE, the responsible party must populate the following sections based on the project context (ensure parameters.md is referenced for global project variables):

  • Sprint or Iteration: The sprint or iteration this retrospective covers. A retrospective that does not say which sprint it belongs to cannot be compared with the previous one, and an uncountable sequence of retrospectives is the same as none.
  • Team Members Present: Who took part. Someone who is not in the room cannot act on what was agreed, so name the absent members and how the outcome will reach them.
  • Date: The date the retrospective was held. Record it against the sprint number on the same line, because a retrospective carrying only a date cannot be matched to the one before it, and the set becomes a list of dates with no context.
  • Start: Actions and behaviors the team will begin to implement. Be specific: "hold a joint review with QA twice a week" can be started, "communicate better" cannot.
  • Stop: Actions or behaviors the team will cease doing. If the team is not willing to actually stop it, recording it here only builds a list the team learns to distrust.
  • Keep: Practices the team should continue with. Note why, because the reason is what a future team will need when the person who introduced the practice has moved on.
  • More: Practices that were not done consistently and should be done more often. Inconsistent usually means the practice exists but nothing enforces it, so record what would enforce it.
  • Less: Practices that were done too much or should be reduced. Watch for process that exists to fix a problem which no longer occurs; that is the usual source of ceremony the team has stopped noticing.
  • Action: The specific change being made, taken from the Start, Stop, More, and Less columns rather than invented separately.
  • Owner: The one person accountable for making it happen. A team cannot own an action, because a team is never available.
  • By When: The date it should be done, and where it will be reviewed. An action with no review date is an action that will be carried into the next retrospective as a note about doing it better.
  • Outcome: What happened when it was tried, filled in at the next retrospective. Without this column the team repeats the same actions and the retrospective becomes a ritual rather than a feedback loop.
  • Future Considerations: The FLAP alternative to the starfish. If the team prefers FLAP, replace the five starfish columns with Accomplishments, Problems, Lessons, and Future Considerations rather than recording both, since two parallel forms get half-filled and neither is trusted.

docs.title: Project Artifact: Prompt Library Log
docs.text:
Document Reference: PMO-05.09

This document provides a comprehensive, professional reference to understand the purpose and effective usage of the Prompt Library Log in alignment with the Tasleemat framework.

docs.title: 1. What?
docs.text: A table of the prompts in use, one row each: an identifier, the use case, the text as it is actually sent, what a good response looks like, and the version and status it currently holds. The text column is the one that decides whether the log is usable: a prompt filed as a description has to be rewritten before it can be sent.

docs.title: 2. Why?
docs.text: Because prompts are written repeatedly and rarely remembered, and the cost of a badly written prompt is paid in the review of whatever it produced. A library converts that cost into a lookup. It also converts an individual judgement into a shared one: a prompt that two people use gets better in a way that one person's habit does not, and the expected output column is what lets a team say the improvement happened.

docs.title: 3. When?
docs.text: Written when a prompt has been used and found worth keeping, and revised whenever the prompt itself is revised. The version belongs in the first entry rather than being added later, because a prompt revised without a version number leaves every earlier result attached to a text that no longer exists.

docs.title: 4. Who?
docs.text: Kept by whoever uses the prompts, which on an AI-enabled project is the team rather than a single owner. The AI or ML lead signs because that role is where prompts are drawn from and where the ones that do not work get noticed. The data protection officer signs because a prompt is where personal data most often enters a model without being noticed.

docs.title: Tailoring Tips
docs.text:
• File the prompt, not its history. The library is read under time pressure, and an entry written with a paragraph of reasoning attached to it is an entry nobody opens.
  • Write the expected output before the prompt is used. Deciding what a good answer looks like after seeing the answer is not a standard, it is a description.
  • Retire what does not work. An entry that was used and did not help is the most valuable line in the log, provided it is marked as one rather than deleted.

docs.title: 1. Pre-requisites & Inputs (Upstream Dependencies)
docs.text:

    • Approved Baselines (Scope/Schedule/Cost)

    • Risk Register (PMO-04.08.02)
    • Stakeholder Engagement Plan (PMO-04.10.01)

docs.title: 2. Downstream Dependents
docs.text:
• Mandatory:

    • Change Log (PMO-05.04)
    • Lessons Learned Summary (PMO-07.01)
  • Optional / Contextual:
    • Variance Analysis (PMO-06.04)
    • Decision Log (PMO-05.02)

docs.title: 5. How?
docs.text:
To accurately complete the Prompt Library Log, populate the following sections based on the project context (ensuring reference to parameters.md for the general project variables):

  • Prompt ID: A short identifier, so a prompt can be referred to in a meeting without its text being read out. A number is enough if it is the only one in use.
  • Use Case: What the prompt is for, in one line: the task it was written to do and the situation it was written in. A prompt filed without its use case cannot be told apart from another one that reads almost the same.
  • Prompt Text: The prompt as it is actually sent, not a description of it. What is filed here has to be usable by pasting it, because a paraphrase is a different prompt and will behave differently.
  • Expected Output: What a good answer looks like, specifically enough to be checked. This is the column that makes the library auditable: without it there is nothing to compare a later response against.
  • Status/Version: Where the prompt stands, and which version this is. A prompt that has been revised without the version moving leaves every earlier result attached to a text that no longer exists.

docs.title: Project Artifact: Impediment Log
docs.text:
Document Reference: PMO-05.10

This document provides a comprehensive, professional reference to understand the purpose and effective usage of the Impediment Log in alignment with the Tasleemat framework.

docs.title: 1. What?
docs.text: A table of the things standing between the team and its work, one row each: an identifier, the date it was raised, what it is, what it costs while it stands, who is pursuing it, and whether it is open, in progress or resolved. The owner column is the one that distinguishes this from an issue list, because it names the person chasing the obstacle rather than the person blocked by it.

docs.title: 2. Why?
docs.text: Because an impediment that is absorbed is an impediment that is hidden. A team that works around one looks productive for exactly as long as the workaround holds, and the cost of the workaround arrives later and separately, where nobody connects it to the decision not to ask. The log also accumulates something an issue list does not: a record of how each one was cleared, which is the part the next team can actually use.

docs.title: 3. When?
docs.text: Raised as soon as it is recognised, and not batched to the end of the cycle. The date it was raised is what makes a stale one visible, because an entry with no date is one nobody can tell has been sitting there. It is closed when the impediment is gone, not when it stops being inconvenient.

docs.title: 4. Who?
docs.text: Raised by whoever hits it, which on an agile team is any member rather than the lead. That is the point of the form: the person nearest an obstacle is the one best placed to name it, and a log that only the lead writes is a log of what the lead noticed. The team lead signs because escalation is their responsibility, and the project manager signs because most impediments can only be cleared above the team.

docs.title: Tailoring Tips
docs.text:
• Raise it rather than absorb it. The workaround is cheaper this cycle and it hides the cost, which is the whole reason the cost is not being argued about.
  • Name the cost, not the annoyance. An entry that says the work is blocked without saying what it costs cannot be weighed against the other things that need the same person.
  • Write the resolution. The entry closes when the impediment is gone, and the note about how it went is the part anyone can reuse.

docs.title: 1. Pre-requisites & Inputs (Upstream Dependencies)
docs.text:
• Mandatory:
    • Project Management Plan (PMO-04.01.01)
    • Approved Baselines (Scope/Schedule/Cost)
  • Optional / Contextual:
    • Risk Register (PMO-04.08.02)
    • Stakeholder Engagement Plan (PMO-04.10.01)

docs.title: 2. Downstream Dependents
docs.text:
• Mandatory:
    • Project Status Reports (PMO-06.01)
    • Change Log (PMO-05.04)
    • Lessons Learned Summary (PMO-07.01)
  • Optional / Contextual:
    • Variance Analysis (PMO-06.04)
    • Decision Log (PMO-05.02)

docs.title: 5. How?
docs.text:
To accurately complete the Impediment Log, populate the following sections based on the project context (ensuring reference to parameters.md for the general project variables):

  • Impediment ID: A short identifier, so an impediment can be referred to in a stand-up without being described again. A number is enough if it is the only one in use.
  • Date Raised: When it was identified. The date is what makes an old impediment visible: an entry with no date is one nobody can tell has been sitting there.
  • Description: What is standing between the team and the work, in terms someone outside the team would understand. A description the reader can only decode by asking is not one that can be escalated.
  • Impact: What it costs while it stands: the work it holds up and what that costs in the cycle. An impediment with no stated impact cannot be prioritised against anything else.
  • Owner: Who is pursuing the resolution, which is not the same as who the impediment affects. The person raising it may be pursuing it and the person who can remove it may be elsewhere.
  • Status: Open, in progress, or resolved, and the date it was resolved. A resolved entry with no resolution recorded is worth little, because the next team to hit it cannot use what was learned.

docs.title: Project Artifact: Meeting Minutes
docs.text:
Document Reference: PMO-05.11

This document provides a comprehensive, professional reference to understand the purpose and effective usage of the Meeting Minutes in alignment with the Tasleemat framework.

docs.title: 1. What?
docs.text: Five things, in the order a reader needs them: what the meeting was called to settle, who was there, what was discussed and why, what was agreed, and what was assigned to whom by when. The last is a table because that is the only form in which an assignment survives being read a week later, when the owner and the date are the two things a paragraph has already lost.

docs.title: 2. Why?
docs.text: Because a meeting is a decision-making device, and a decision that was not written down did not happen as far as anyone outside the room is concerned. The minutes also settle a question that comes up repeatedly, which is what was weighed. A decision taken over an objection is a decision somebody will reopen, and the objection is the part that tells you whether reopening it is reasonable.

docs.title: 3. When?
docs.text: Written while the meeting is being held or immediately after it, not at the end of the week, because the value of the record decays with every hour it is not written down. The discussion is recorded as the reasoning, not the speech: what was said has almost no bearing on what was agreed, and a record of the speech cannot be read later.

docs.title: 4. Who?
docs.text: Written by whoever took the notes, which is not always the chair, and approved by the chair before it is circulated. The chair signs because a minute that records a decision as agreed commits the chair to having put it to the room. The project manager signs because most of what a project meeting decides lands in the project record rather than staying in the file.

docs.title: Tailoring Tips
docs.text:
• Write the decisions, not the discussion. Most of what was said has no bearing on what was agreed, and minutes that record the speech cannot be read by anybody afterwards.
  • Name an owner and a date or write nothing. An action item with neither is a topic for the next meeting, and topics accumulate until the meeting is cancelled for lack of them.
  • Record the objection. A decision taken over a stated objection is one that will be reopened, and the objection is what tells you whether that matters this time.

docs.title: 1. Pre-requisites & Inputs (Upstream Dependencies)
docs.text:
• Mandatory:
    • Project Management Plan (PMO-04.01.01)
    • Approved Baselines (Scope/Schedule/Cost)
  • Optional / Contextual:
    • Risk Register (PMO-04.08.02)
    • Stakeholder Engagement Plan (PMO-04.10.01)

docs.title: 2. Downstream Dependents
docs.text:
• Mandatory:
    • Project Status Reports (PMO-06.01)
    • Change Log (PMO-05.04)
    • Lessons Learned Summary (PMO-07.01)
  • Optional / Contextual:
    • Variance Analysis (PMO-06.04)
    • Decision Log (PMO-05.02)

docs.title: 5. How?
docs.text:
To accurately complete the Meeting Minutes, populate the following sections based on the project context (ensuring reference to parameters.md for the general project variables):

  • Meeting Objective: What the meeting was called to settle, in one sentence. A purpose written after the meeting is a summary, and it is the only line that tells a reader whether anything was decided.
  • Attendees: Who was there, and who sent apologies. The list is not administrative: it is what tells a later reader whose agreement a decision carries, and who has to be told when the position changes.
  • Key Discussion Points: The matters discussed, with the reasoning recorded alongside the conclusion. A decision with no recorded reasoning is one that gets relitigated, because the next person cannot see what was weighed.
  • Decisions Made: What was agreed, one per entry, attributed to the meeting that agreed it. This section is the one that is read later, and anything not written here did not happen as far as the record is concerned.
  • Action Items: What was assigned, to whom, and by when. Written as a table because a task in a paragraph has no owner and no deadline a week later, and an action item without those two is a note.

docs.title: Project Artifact: Team Onboarding Checklist
docs.text:
Document Reference: PMO-05.12

This document provides a comprehensive, professional reference to understand the purpose and effective usage of the Team Onboarding Checklist in alignment with the Tasleemat framework.

docs.title: 1. What?
docs.text: A table of the steps that have to happen before somebody can be useful, one row each: the task written so its completion is checkable, who does it, when it should be done, and whether it is done. The dates are relative to the joining date rather than to a calendar day, because the joining date moves and a checklist full of fixed dates has to be redone every time it does.

docs.title: 2. Why?
docs.text: Because the steps that are missed are the ones nobody can see are missing. A new member without access does not raise a problem, they sit quietly, and the team's interpretation is that they are taking a while to settle. Written down, the same list serves the second person, the fifth person and the person who joined while two others were on leave.

docs.title: 3. When?
docs.text: Started on the joining date and closed when the last entry is done, which is normally the end of the first week. It is also reopened whenever somebody joins mid-cycle, because the checklist is per person and not per project, and a checklist written for the first joiner is not automatically true for the second.

docs.title: 4. Who?
docs.text: Owned by whoever is responsible for the new member's first week, which on most projects is the team lead rather than the project manager. That is worth being explicit about, because the tasks themselves mostly belong to other people: access is granted by whoever administers it, the tooling introduction is given by whoever knows it best, and neither of them is the team lead. The checklist exists so that the team lead knows they have been asked.

docs.title: Tailoring Tips
docs.text:
• Write what done looks like, not what to do. A task nobody can mark as complete is a task nobody completes, and "get set up" is the commonest example of one.
  • Name the one-off. Most of these are a single action by a single person, and the step that gets missed is almost always one that belongs to somebody outside the team who was never told.
  • Close the checklist. The last entry is the one that says the onboarding is finished, and without it the list has no end and the status column stops meaning anything.

docs.title: 1. Pre-requisites & Inputs (Upstream Dependencies)
docs.text:
• Mandatory:
    • Project Management Plan (PMO-04.01.01)
    • Approved Baselines (Scope/Schedule/Cost)
  • Optional / Contextual:
    • Risk Register (PMO-04.08.02)
    • Stakeholder Engagement Plan (PMO-04.10.01)

docs.title: 2. Downstream Dependents
docs.text:
• Mandatory:
    • Project Status Reports (PMO-06.01)
    • Change Log (PMO-05.04)
    • Lessons Learned Summary (PMO-07.01)
  • Optional / Contextual:
    • Variance Analysis (PMO-06.04)
    • Decision Log (PMO-05.02)

docs.title: 5. How?
docs.text:
To accurately complete the Team Onboarding Checklist, populate the following sections based on the project context (ensuring reference to parameters.md for the general project variables):

  • Task: The activity, written so that a person who does not know the project can tell whether it is done. "Get set up" is not a task; "reviewed the onboarding document" is.
  • Assigned To: Who does it, which is not the same as who is waiting for it. Most onboarding tasks are somebody's one-off action, and naming the one-off is what stops the new member chasing something nobody owns.
  • Due Date: When it should be complete, relative to the joining date rather than to a calendar day, because the joining date moves and a checklist full of fixed dates has to be redone when it does.
  • Status: Done or pending, and the date it was done. A checklist nobody updates is one that has quietly stopped being true, and the entry is what shows it has.

docs.title: Project Artifact: Project Status Report
docs.text:
Document Reference: PMO-06.01

This document provides a comprehensive, professional reference to understand the purpose and effective usage of the Project Status Report in alignment with the Tasleemat framework.

docs.title: 1. What?
docs.text: A formal executive artifact presenting regular performance metrics, milestones, risks, and forecasts across the project.

docs.title: 2. Why?
docs.text: Enables executive sponsors and PMO leaders to make informed governance decisions and authorize necessary interventions.

docs.title: 3. When?
docs.text: Prepared on a recurring cycle (weekly or monthly) throughout executing, monitoring, and controlling phases.

docs.title: 4. Who?
docs.text: Authored by the Project Manager and distributed to Project Sponsors, PMO Director, and Steering Committees.

docs.title: Tailoring Tips
docs.text:
• Adjust reporting frequency and level of detail based on project scale, risk rating, and stakeholder governance needs.
  • Emphasize variance root causes and corrective action plans rather than raw descriptive status.

docs.title: 1. Pre-requisites & Inputs (Upstream Dependencies)
docs.text:
• Mandatory:
    • Approved Project Baselines (PMO-04.01.01)
    • Work Performance Data & Logs (PMO-05.01 - 05.12)
  • Optional / Contextual:
    • Risk Register (PMO-04.08.02)
    • Vendor Agreements (PMO-04.09.04)

docs.title: 2. Downstream Dependents
docs.text:
• Mandatory:
    • Change Requests (PMO-05.03)
    • Project / Phase Closeout (PMO-07.03)
    • Lessons Learned Summary (PMO-07.01)
  • Optional / Contextual:
    • Transition to Operations Checklist (PMO-07.04)
    • Value Realization Register (PMO-01.03)

docs.title: 5. How?
docs.text:
To accurately and professionally complete the Project Status Report, the responsible party must populate the following critical sections based on the project context (ensure parameters.md is referenced for global project variables):

  • Accomplishments for this reporting period: Key milestones, deliverables, and tasks completed during this period.
  • Accomplishments planned but not completed this reporting period: Activities that were scheduled for completion but remain in progress or delayed.
  • Root cause of schedule variances: Underlying causes and contributing factors for any schedule delays or slippages.
  • Impact to upcoming milestones or project due date: Expected effects of current schedule performance on future critical path milestones.
  • Planned corrective or preventive action (Schedule): Specific recovery actions planned to bring the schedule back in alignment with baseline.
  • Funds spent this reporting period: Total expenditures and actual costs incurred during the current reporting period.
  • Root cause of cost variances: Reasons for any cost overruns or underruns compared against the cost baseline.
  • Impact to overall budget or contingency funds: Projected impact of current spending trends on total project budget and reserves.
  • Planned corrective or preventive action (Cost): Corrective steps designed to control project expenditure within approved budget limits.
  • Accomplishments planned for next reporting period: Key objectives, tasks, and deliverables scheduled for execution in the next cycle.
  • Costs planned for next reporting period: Anticipated financial expenditures and commitments for the upcoming period.
  • New risks identified: Newly discovered risks requiring qualitative or quantitative analysis and response planning.
  • New issues identified: Newly materialized issues requiring immediate tracking and resolution.
  • Escalations: Matters requiring immediate intervention or decision-making from executive sponsors.
  • Decisions made: Significant architectural, operational, or management decisions ratified during this period.
  • Change requests submitted this period: Summary of formal change requests submitted, evaluated, or approved this period.
  • Lessons learned and knowledge transfer: Insights and practical lessons captured to enhance ongoing and future project performance.
  • Comments: Additional explanatory notes, contextual remarks, or qualitative updates.

docs.title: Project Artifact: Team Member Status Report
docs.text:
Document Reference: PMO-06.02

This document provides a comprehensive, professional reference to understand the purpose and effective usage of the Team Member Status Report in alignment with the Tasleemat framework.

docs.title: 1. What?
docs.text: A structured status report completed by team members detailing personal deliverables, effort, quality, and blockers.

docs.title: 2. Why?
docs.text: Provides granular visibility into work package progress and surfaces micro-level risks before they impact major milestones.

docs.title: 3. When?
docs.text: Completed on a regular cadence (weekly or bi-weekly) during project executing and monitoring phases.

docs.title: 4. Who?
docs.text: Authored by individual project contributors or technical leads and submitted to the Project Manager or Team Lead.

docs.title: Tailoring Tips
docs.text:
• Simplify or omit cost fields for internal resources where tracking is managed centrally.
  • Focus on blocker resolution and dependency alignment for Agile sprints.

docs.title: 1. Pre-requisites & Inputs (Upstream Dependencies)
docs.text:
• Mandatory:
    • Approved Project Baselines (PMO-04.01.01)
    • Work Performance Data & Logs (PMO-05.01 - 05.12)
  • Optional / Contextual:
    • Risk Register (PMO-04.08.02)
    • Vendor Agreements (PMO-04.09.04)

docs.title: 2. Downstream Dependents
docs.text:
• Mandatory:
    • Change Requests (PMO-05.03)
    • Project / Phase Closeout (PMO-07.03)
    • Lessons Learned Summary (PMO-07.01)
  • Optional / Contextual:
    • Transition to Operations Checklist (PMO-07.04)
    • Value Realization Register (PMO-01.03)

docs.title: 5. How?
docs.text:
To accurately and professionally complete the Team Member Status Report, the responsible party must populate the following critical sections based on the project context (ensure parameters.md is referenced for global project variables):

  • Activities planned this reporting period: Tasks and work packages scheduled for execution by this member during this period.
  • Activities accomplished this reporting period: Tasks and work packages successfully finalized by this member during this period.
  • Activities planned but not accomplished this reporting period: Scheduled tasks that were started but not completed or deferred.
  • Root cause of schedule variances: Underlying reasons for any task delays or workload obstacles.
  • Funds planned to be spent this reporting period: Planned labor hours or direct expenses allocated for the member this period.
  • Funds spent this reporting period: Actual labor hours or expenses incurred by the member during this period.
  • Root cause of cost variances: Reasons for discrepancies between planned and actual resource expenditures.
  • Quality variances identified this period: Defects, rework, or non-conformance issues encountered in deliverables.
  • Planned corrective or preventive action: Targeted remedial steps to correct quality issues or prevent recurring defects.
  • Activities planned for next reporting period: Upcoming work assignments and deliverables scheduled for the next interval.
  • Costs planned for next reporting period: Estimated hours or expenditures planned for the upcoming reporting period.
  • New risks identified: Potential technical, operational, or resource uncertainties identified by the member.
  • New issues identified: Immediate roadblocks, blockers, or dependencies requiring team resolution.
  • Escalations: Impediments requiring intervention from the Project Manager or Team Lead.
  • Decisions made: Technical or operational choices adopted by the team member during execution.
  • Lessons learned and knowledge transfer: Practical findings and best practices captured during task execution.
  • Comments: Additional reflections, notes, or contextual feedback from the team member.

docs.title: Project Artifact: Contractor Status Report
docs.text:
Document Reference: PMO-06.03

This document provides a comprehensive, professional reference to understand the purpose and effective usage of the Contractor Status Report in alignment with the Tasleemat framework.

docs.title: 1. What?
docs.text: A structured periodic performance report prepared by contractors to account for deliverable progress, cost, quality, and claims.

docs.title: 2. Why?
docs.text: Ensures contractual compliance, tracks vendor performance objectively, and provides early warning on procurement delays.

docs.title: 3. When?
docs.text: Submitted at agreed contractual intervals (e.g., monthly) during the procurement execution phase.

docs.title: 4. Who?
docs.text: Authored by Contractor Project Manager or Representative and reviewed by Project Manager and Procurement Lead.

docs.title: Tailoring Tips
docs.text:
• Omit cost forecasts for fixed-price contracts where total pricing is not subject to cost reimbursement.
  • Include quantitative EVM metrics for complex turnkey contractor engagements.

docs.title: 1. Pre-requisites & Inputs (Upstream Dependencies)
docs.text:
• Mandatory:
    • Approved Project Baselines (PMO-04.01.01)
    • Work Performance Data & Logs (PMO-05.01 - 05.12)
  • Optional / Contextual:
    • Risk Register (PMO-04.08.02)
    • Vendor Agreements (PMO-04.09.04)

docs.title: 2. Downstream Dependents
docs.text:
• Mandatory:
    • Change Requests (PMO-05.03)
    • Project / Phase Closeout (PMO-07.03)
    • Lessons Learned Summary (PMO-07.01)
  • Optional / Contextual:
    • Transition to Operations Checklist (PMO-07.04)
    • Value Realization Register (PMO-01.03)

docs.title: 5. How?
docs.text:
To accurately and professionally complete the Contractor Status Report, the responsible party must populate the following critical sections based on the project context (ensure parameters.md is referenced for global project variables):

  • Contractor: The legal name and contact details of the contractor performing the contract.
  • Contract Number and Type: The official contract identifier and contract type (e.g., Fixed Price, T&M).
  • Reporting Period: The start and end calendar dates covered by this contractor report.
  • Report Submission Date: The exact date on which the report was officially submitted to the project manager.
  • Scope / Status This Period: Assessment of contracted scope deliverables completed or in progress during this period.
  • Scope / Variance and Cause: Explanation of any deviations from contracted scope baselines and their root causes.
  • Quality / Status This Period: Evaluation of deliverable quality against contracted standards and specifications.
  • Quality / Variance and Cause: Root causes and details of any non-conformance or failed quality checks.
  • Schedule / Status This Period: Assessment of progress against contracted milestone dates and schedule baselines.
  • Schedule / Variance and Cause: Root cause explanation for any schedule delays or accelerations.
  • Cost / Status This Period: Assessment of contract billings and expenditures against the financial plan.
  • Cost / Variance and Cause: Root cause explanation for any financial variances or billing discrepancies.
  • Estimated Completion Date / Estimate: The contractor projected delivery and contract completion date.
  • Estimated Completion Date / Basis: Basis and rationale supporting the estimated completion date.
  • Estimated Final Cost / Estimate: Projected total final cost at completion (applicable to cost-reimbursable contracts).
  • Estimated Final Cost / Basis: Basis and historical cost rate data supporting the estimated final cost.
  • Key Forecast Assumptions / Estimate: Summary of key assumptions underpinning forecast values.
  • Key Forecast Assumptions / Basis: Dependencies and external conditions supporting forecast stability.
  • Claims or Disputes: Summary of any new, pending, or resolved contractual claims or disputes.
  • Risks: Key vendor-side risks that could impact contract milestones or deliverables.
  • Planned Corrective or Preventive Action: Specific remedial actions planned by the contractor to recover performance variances.
  • Issues: Current active roadblocks, technical issues, or dependencies affecting execution.
  • Escalations: Items requiring urgent decisions or dispute intervention from the buyer or PMO.
  • Contract Change Requests: Summary of formal contract change proposals submitted, reviewed, or pending.
  • Comments: Additional context, contractor remarks, or explanatory notes.

docs.title: Project Artifact: Variance Analysis
docs.text:
Document Reference: PMO-06.04

This document provides a comprehensive, professional reference to understand the purpose and effective usage of the Variance Analysis in alignment with the Tasleemat framework.

docs.title: 1. What?
docs.text: A structured analysis report identifying variances, diagnosing root causes, and formulating corrective actions.

docs.title: 2. Why?
docs.text: Enables timely diagnostic understanding of project deviations and provides defensible evidence for corrective actions.

docs.title: 3. When?
docs.text: Conducted periodically or upon detecting threshold breaches during monitoring and controlling.

docs.title: 4. Who?
docs.text: Prepared by the Project Manager with Project Controllers and reviewed by PMO and Governance committees.

docs.title: Tailoring Tips
docs.text:
• Set custom variance tolerance thresholds (e.g., +/- 5% cost or schedule) to trigger formal root-cause analysis.
  • Combine with Earned Value forecasting for capital-intensive infrastructure and engineering projects.

docs.title: 1. Pre-requisites & Inputs (Upstream Dependencies)
docs.text:
• Mandatory:
    • Approved Project Baselines (PMO-04.01.01)
    • Work Performance Data & Logs (PMO-05.01 - 05.12)
  • Optional / Contextual:
    • Risk Register (PMO-04.08.02)
    • Vendor Agreements (PMO-04.09.04)

docs.title: 2. Downstream Dependents
docs.text:
• Mandatory:
    • Change Requests (PMO-05.03)
    • Project / Phase Closeout (PMO-07.03)
    • Lessons Learned Summary (PMO-07.01)
  • Optional / Contextual:
    • Transition to Operations Checklist (PMO-07.04)
    • Value Realization Register (PMO-01.03)

docs.title: 5. How?
docs.text:
To accurately and professionally complete the Variance Analysis, the responsible party must populate the following critical sections based on the project context (ensure parameters.md is referenced for global project variables):

  • Schedule / Planned Result: The target baseline schedule milestone, duration, or date.
  • Schedule / Actual Result: The actual completed milestone date, duration, or current progress.
  • Schedule / Variance: Calculated difference between actual schedule performance and the baseline.
  • Schedule / Root Cause: Primary cause and contributing factors for schedule variance.
  • Schedule / Planned Response: Action plan or recovery strategy designed to address schedule variance.
  • Cost / Planned Result: The approved baseline budget or planned expenditure for the period.
  • Cost / Actual Result: The actual expenditures or costs incurred during the period.
  • Cost / Variance: Calculated difference between actual expenditures and the cost baseline.
  • Cost / Root Cause: Primary drivers and events resulting in cost overruns or savings.
  • Cost / Planned Response: Corrective measures and cost containment actions to realign with budget.
  • Quality / Planned Result: The quality metric, acceptance threshold, or standard expected.
  • Quality / Actual Result: The actual measured quality outcome, defect rate, or test score.
  • Quality / Variance: Discrepancy between actual quality achievements and defined quality metrics.
  • Quality / Root Cause: Root cause analysis detailing why quality requirements were not met.
  • Quality / Planned Response: Remediation plan, rework procedures, or process improvements.
  • Scope / Planned Result: The authorized deliverables and work packages committed in the scope statement.
  • Scope / Actual Result: The actual scope deliverables completed and verified during the period.
  • Scope / Variance: Extent of scope variance, unapproved scope additions, or unfinished deliverables.
  • Scope / Root Cause: Factors causing scope variance, creep, or delayed deliverable completions.
  • Scope / Planned Response: Corrective actions, change requests, or realignment to baseline scope.
  • Implications of continued variance (Forecast): Anticipated long-term impact on overall project objectives if variances persist.
  • Escalation Required (Y/N): Clear indication (Yes/No) whether senior leadership escalation is necessary.
  • Escalation Details: Details of the specific escalation path, required decisions, and target stakeholders.
  • Comments: Additional explanatory notes, cross-functional dependencies, or contextual insights.

docs.title: Project Artifact: Earned Value Analysis
docs.text:
Document Reference: PMO-06.05

This document provides a comprehensive, professional reference to understand the purpose and effective usage of the Earned Value Analysis in alignment with the Tasleemat framework.

docs.title: 1. What?
docs.text: A quantitative management artifact calculating PV, EV, AC, variances (SV, CV), indices (SPI, CPI), and estimates at completion (EAC, TCPI).

docs.title: 2. Why?
docs.text: Provides objective mathematical forecasting of final project cost and completion dates, avoiding optimistic bias.

docs.title: 3. When?
docs.text: Calculated at regular reporting intervals throughout project execution and controlling.

docs.title: 4. Who?
docs.text: Produced by Project Controller or Project Manager and reviewed by PMO and Executive Sponsors.

docs.title: Tailoring Tips
docs.text:
• Select the appropriate EAC forecasting formula based on whether past variances are considered typical or atypical.
  • Calculate EVM at control account level for complex multi-vendor programs.

docs.title: 1. Pre-requisites & Inputs (Upstream Dependencies)
docs.text:
• Mandatory:
    • Approved Project Baselines (PMO-04.01.01)
    • Work Performance Data & Logs (PMO-05.01 - 05.12)
  • Optional / Contextual:
    • Risk Register (PMO-04.08.02)
    • Vendor Agreements (PMO-04.09.04)

docs.title: 2. Downstream Dependents
docs.text:
• Mandatory:
    • Change Requests (PMO-05.03)
    • Project / Phase Closeout (PMO-07.03)
    • Lessons Learned Summary (PMO-07.01)
  • Optional / Contextual:
    • Transition to Operations Checklist (PMO-07.04)
    • Value Realization Register (PMO-01.03)

docs.title: 5. How?
docs.text:
To accurately and professionally complete the Earned Value Analysis, the responsible party must populate the following critical sections based on the project context (ensure parameters.md is referenced for global project variables):

  • Budget at Completion (BAC): The total approved baseline budget allocated for the complete project scope.
  • Planned Value (PV) / Current Reporting Period: The authorized budget assigned to scheduled work for the current reporting period.
  • Planned Value (PV) / Current Period Cumulative: The cumulative authorized budget planned from project start through current period.
  • Planned Value (PV) / Past Period Cumulative: The cumulative planned value calculated at the close of the previous reporting period.
  • Earned Value (EV) / Current Reporting Period: The budgeted amount for the work actually completed during the current period.
  • Earned Value (EV) / Current Period Cumulative: The cumulative budgeted amount for all work accomplished from project start to date.
  • Earned Value (EV) / Past Period Cumulative: The cumulative earned value achieved as of the previous reporting period.
  • Actual Cost (AC) / Current Reporting Period: The actual expenditures incurred for work performed during the current period.
  • Actual Cost (AC) / Current Period Cumulative: The cumulative total actual costs incurred from project start through current period.
  • Actual Cost (AC) / Past Period Cumulative: The cumulative actual costs recorded as of the previous reporting period.
  • Schedule Variance (SV) / Current Reporting Period: The schedule performance in financial terms (EV - PV) for the current period.
  • Schedule Variance (SV) / Current Period Cumulative: The cumulative schedule variance (Cumulative EV - Cumulative PV) to date.
  • Schedule Variance (SV) / Past Period Cumulative: The cumulative schedule variance as of the prior reporting period.
  • Cost Variance (CV) / Current Reporting Period: The financial budget variance (EV - AC) for the current reporting period.
  • Cost Variance (CV) / Current Period Cumulative: The cumulative cost variance (Cumulative EV - Cumulative AC) to date.
  • Cost Variance (CV) / Past Period Cumulative: The cumulative cost variance as of the prior reporting period.
  • Schedule Performance Index (SPI) / Current Reporting Period: The schedule efficiency ratio (EV / PV) for the current period.
  • Schedule Performance Index (SPI) / Current Period Cumulative: The cumulative schedule efficiency ratio (Cumulative EV / Cumulative PV).
  • Schedule Performance Index (SPI) / Past Period Cumulative: The cumulative schedule efficiency index from the previous reporting period.
  • Cost Performance Index (CPI) / Current Reporting Period: The cost efficiency ratio (EV / AC) for the current period.
  • Cost Performance Index (CPI) / Current Period Cumulative: The cumulative cost efficiency ratio (Cumulative EV / Cumulative AC).
  • Cost Performance Index (CPI) / Past Period Cumulative: The cumulative cost efficiency index from the previous reporting period.
  • Percent Planned / Current Reporting Period: Planned Value divided by BAC for the current reporting period.
  • Percent Planned / Current Period Cumulative: Cumulative Planned Value divided by BAC to measure scheduled completion percentage.
  • Percent Planned / Past Period Cumulative: Cumulative Planned Value divided by BAC as of the prior reporting period.
  • Percent Earned / Current Reporting Period: Earned Value divided by BAC for the current reporting period.
  • Percent Earned / Current Period Cumulative: Cumulative Earned Value divided by BAC representing actual project percent complete.
  • Percent Earned / Past Period Cumulative: Cumulative Earned Value divided by BAC as of the prior reporting period.
  • Percent Spent / Current Reporting Period: Actual Cost divided by BAC for the current reporting period.
  • Percent Spent / Current Period Cumulative: Cumulative Actual Cost divided by BAC representing total project budget spent to date.
  • Percent Spent / Past Period Cumulative: Cumulative Actual Cost divided by BAC as of the prior reporting period.
  • EAC w/CPI / Current Reporting Period: Estimate at Completion assuming future work performed at current period CPI (BAC / CPI).
  • EAC w/CPI / Current Period Cumulative: Estimate at Completion assuming future work performed at cumulative CPI.
  • EAC w/CPI / Past Period Cumulative: Estimate at Completion based on past period cumulative CPI.
  • EAC w/CPI × SPI / Current Reporting Period: Estimate at Completion factoring both cost and schedule indices for current period.
  • EAC w/CPI × SPI / Current Period Cumulative: Estimate at Completion factoring cumulative cost and schedule performance indices.
  • EAC w/CPI × SPI / Past Period Cumulative: Estimate at Completion factoring past period cumulative cost and schedule indices.
  • To Complete Performance Index (TCPI) / Current Reporting Period: Cost efficiency required to complete the remaining work within BAC for current period.
  • To Complete Performance Index (TCPI) / Current Period Cumulative: Cost efficiency required to complete the remaining work within BAC cumulatively.
  • To Complete Performance Index (TCPI) / Past Period Cumulative: TCPI calculated at the close of the prior reporting period.
  • Selected EAC - Justification and Explanation: Detailed justification of the selected EAC forecasting formula and expected final budget outcome.
  • Root cause of schedule variance: Underlying drivers and operational causes for schedule efficiency or delay.
  • Schedule impact (incl. implications of continued variance): Projected delivery delays and critical path impacts if schedule trends continue.
  • Root cause of cost variance: Operational factors, rate fluctuations, or scope drivers causing cost variances.
  • Budget impact (incl. intended actions/reserves): Financial exposure and reserve utilization strategies to maintain fiscal control.
  • Comments: Additional contextual observations or recommendations from the EVM analyst.

docs.text:

This document provides a comprehensive, professional reference to understand the purpose and effective usage of the Risk Audit in alignment with the Tasleemat framework.

docs.title: 1. What?
docs.text: A structured audit report assessing compliance with risk processes and analyzing the efficacy of risk response strategies.

docs.title: 2. Why?
docs.text: Ensures continuous improvement in risk identification and verifies that organizational risk policies are followed.

docs.title: 3. When?
docs.text: Conducted periodically at designated milestones or upon major risk triggers during project execution.

docs.title: 4. Who?
docs.text: Conducted by an independent Risk Auditor or PMO Lead and submitted to the Project Manager and Governance Board.

docs.title: Tailoring Tips
docs.text:
• Scale audit depth based on project risk classification and regulatory compliance requirements.
  • Focus on recurring operational risk patterns in iterative sprint retrospectives.

docs.title: Artifact: Product Acceptance Form
docs.text:
Document Reference: PMO-06.08

This document provides a detailed, professional reference for understanding the purpose of the Product Acceptance Form and using it effectively as part of the Tasleemat methodology.

docs.title: 1. What is it?
docs.text: An official Tasleemat document called the Product Acceptance Form, used to record the acceptance of each deliverable or component as it is validated. It is part of process 5.5 Validate Scope in the PMBOK Guide - Sixth Edition, and should be done periodically throughout the project life cycle.

docs.title: 2. Why?
docs.text: To ensure alignment with Tasleemat standards, to provide transparency, to evidence that deliverables meet the agreed requirements, and to tie acceptance to the requirements documentation and the requirements traceability matrix.

docs.title: 3. When?
docs.text: This artifact is prepared and updated primarily during the Monitoring and Controlling Process Group of the project lifecycle, as each deliverable is validated and accepted.

docs.title: 4. Who?
docs.text: Responsibilities: Prepared by the project manager or product owner, and signed by the party accepting the product, including the client representative where an external party is involved.

docs.title: Tailoring Tips
docs.text:
• For a small project with only a few deliverables you may not need this form; acceptance may instead be recorded in the project status report.
  • You can add a column to indicate the verification method used to prove that the deliverables meet the requirements. In that case the form becomes a product verification, validation, and acceptance form.

docs.title: Alignment
docs.text:
• Scope management plan
  • Requirements documentation
  • Requirements traceability matrix
  • Quality management plan

docs.title: 5. How?
docs.text:
To accurately and professionally complete the PRODUCT ACCEPTANCE FORM, the responsible party must populate the following critical sections based on the project context (ensure parameters.md is referenced for global project variables):

  • Product Acceptance Record: For each requirement or deliverable accepted, record the ID, the requirement, the acceptance criteria, the validation method, the verification method if used, the status, the sign-off, the acceptance date, and any comments.
  • Comments: Add any comments relevant to the acceptance, such as conditions attached to it or items deferred.

docs.title: Project Artifact: Vendor Performance Scorecard
docs.text:
Document Reference: PMO-06.09

This document provides a comprehensive, professional reference to understand the purpose and effective usage of the Vendor Performance Scorecard in alignment with the Tasleemat framework.

docs.title: 1. What?
docs.text: A table of the measures the project tracks for one supplier, one row each: the metric named so that both sides would recognise it, the target agreed for the period, the score actually measured together with the method, the variance from that target with the direction that matters, and the corrective action with an owner and a date where the variance is a shortfall.

docs.title: 2. Why?
docs.text: Because a score with no target behind it cannot be argued with in either direction. The supplier regards it as good, the project regards it as adequate, and nothing in the document settles the disagreement. Agreeing the target beforehand is what converts the form from a record of an opinion into the basis for a decision, and it is also what makes the variance column worth computing at all.

docs.title: 3. When?
docs.text: Once per period, per supplier, and kept rather than overwritten, because a single period says almost nothing and the trend is what identifies a supplier that is drifting. Reviewed by whoever owns the contract, and read again at closeout, where the question is not how the last quarter went but whether the supplier would be chosen again.

docs.title: 4. Who?
docs.text: Owned by the procurement manager, who holds the contract and is the only party with standing to act on what the numbers show, with the project manager supplying the schedule and quality context the measures come from. The supplier representative signs the record, and that signature is worth having precisely because it means both sides are working from the same figures rather than from two accounts of the same period.

docs.title: Tailoring Tips
docs.text:
• Agree the target before the period starts. A target written afterwards is a description of what happened, and the variance column then computes a gap between the outcome and itself.
  • State the measure with the score. A number whose method changed between periods cannot be compared with one whose method did not, and the comparison is the only reason the number exists.
  • Write a corrective action only where there is a shortfall, and name who owns it. A variance with no response is recorded again next period, because the only thing that changed in between was the number.

docs.title: 1. Pre-requisites & Inputs (Upstream Dependencies)
docs.text:
• Mandatory:
    • Approved Project Baselines (PMO-04.01.01)
    • Work Performance Data & Logs (PMO-05.01 - 05.12)
  • Optional / Contextual:
    • Risk Register (PMO-04.08.02)
    • Vendor Agreements (PMO-04.09.04)

docs.title: 2. Downstream Dependents
docs.text:
• Mandatory:
    • Change Requests (PMO-05.03)
    • Project / Phase Closeout (PMO-07.03)
    • Lessons Learned Summary (PMO-07.01)
  • Optional / Contextual:
    • Transition to Operations Checklist (PMO-07.04)
    • Value Realization Register (PMO-01.03)

docs.title: 5. How?
docs.text:
To accurately complete the Vendor Performance Scorecard, populate the following sections based on the project context (ensuring reference to parameters.md for the general project variables):

  • Metric/KPI: What is being measured, named so that both sides would recognise it. "Quality" is not a metric; "defects found in acceptance, per hundred items delivered" is, because a word cannot be measured twice and compared across periods.
  • Target Score: The level agreed in advance, with the period it applies to. A target written after the result is known is not a target, it is a description, and this column is the one that makes the variance column mean anything.
  • Actual Score: What was measured, and how. The measure is stated with the score so that a later reader can tell whether the same method was used in both periods; a number whose method has changed is not comparable to a number whose method did not.
  • Variance: Target minus actual, with the direction that matters. Whether a positive number is good or bad depends on the metric, and stating it here is what stops the sign being argued about instead of the performance.
  • Corrective Action: What happens because of the variance, and by when. Written only where there is a shortfall, and naming who does it: a scorecard that records a variance and no response produces the same variance next period, because the only thing that changed in between was the number.

docs.title: Project Artifact: User Acceptance Testing Signoff
docs.text:
Document Reference: PMO-06.10

This document provides a comprehensive, professional reference to understand the purpose and effective usage of the User Acceptance Testing Signoff in alignment with the Tasleemat framework.

docs.title: 1. What?
docs.text: Five statements rather than a table, because their lengths are not comparable and a table would pretend they are: what was tested, where it was tested and against what was decided beforehand as the standard for passing, what was found and accepted rather than fixed, and the business's decision in its own terms.

docs.title: 2. Why?
docs.text: Because acceptance is the point at which the work stops being the project's and becomes the business's. A test report can be reopened; a signature cannot be withdrawn by the team that asked for it. That is what makes the record worth keeping carefully, and it is also why the criteria and the defects matter more than they would in a test report: the criteria establish what was actually agreed, and the defects are what the business knew about when it agreed.

docs.title: 3. When?
docs.text: Once per release or per acceptance milestone, after the testing has been executed and before the project moves to the next phase or to operations. Not drafted in advance and not revised afterwards: a signoff edited after a problem is found is a signoff that cannot be relied on, because the reader has no way to tell what was agreed from what was accepted later.

docs.title: 4. Who?
docs.text: Signed by the business owner or client representative, who is the party accepting the risk and is the only one with the authority to accept it, with the quality manager accountable for the testing having been done against the plan and the project manager for the schedule consequence of the date. The client signature is the one that matters and the one most often missing, which is how a project reaches go-live with nobody having agreed to anything.

docs.title: Tailoring Tips
docs.text:
• Agree the criteria before the testing starts. Criteria written afterwards describe what happened rather than deciding whether it was acceptable, and a reader cannot tell the two apart.
  • Record what was accepted, not only what passed. An empty defects section asserts that the testing found nothing, which is almost never what happened, and a reader who suspects that has no way to check it.
  • Say which build and which environment. A pass somewhere other than where the business will work is not a pass, and the signature does not carry that distinction.

docs.title: 1. Pre-requisites & Inputs (Upstream Dependencies)
docs.text:
• Mandatory:
    • Approved Project Baselines (PMO-04.01.01)
    • Work Performance Data & Logs (PMO-05.01 - 05.12)
  • Optional / Contextual:
    • Risk Register (PMO-04.08.02)
    • Vendor Agreements (PMO-04.09.04)

docs.title: 2. Downstream Dependents
docs.text:
• Mandatory:
    • Change Requests (PMO-05.03)
    • Project / Phase Closeout (PMO-07.03)
    • Lessons Learned Summary (PMO-07.01)
  • Optional / Contextual:
    • Transition to Operations Checklist (PMO-07.04)
    • Value Realization Register (PMO-01.03)

docs.title: 5. How?
docs.text:
To accurately complete the User Acceptance Testing Signoff, populate the following sections based on the project context (ensuring reference to parameters.md for the general project variables):

  • Test Summary: What was tested, stated so that a reader can tell whether this was the whole release or a slice of it, and so that the criteria below can be read against something. "The system" is not a test summary; "the three checkout flows plus the refund path" is.
  • Testing Environment: Where the testing took place and against what. The environment and the build are part of what was accepted: a pass on a developer's machine is not a pass on the environment the business will use, and a signature that does not record which one was tested cannot be relied on at go-live.
  • Pass/Fail Criteria: What was decided before the testing began, not what was concluded after it. The criteria are what make the result mean anything: "the system works" cannot fail, because every system works on the day it is demonstrated, and a criterion written afterwards describes the outcome.
  • Known Defects: What was found and accepted rather than fixed, with the severity and who agreed to carry it. This section is what makes the signature honest: an empty defects section says the testing found nothing, which is almost never what happened, and a reader who knows that stops trusting the signature. Anything still open at go-live is discovered by somebody with no authority left to stop it.
  • Business Owner Sign-off: The decision, stated in the business's own terms rather than as a signature alone. What is being accepted, what is being accepted with, and what happens if something turns out not to work. This is the line that is read later when the question is whether the business agreed to this.

docs.title: Project Artifact: Project Health Check Matrix
docs.text:
Document Reference: PMO-06.11

This document provides a comprehensive, professional reference to understand the purpose and effective usage of the Project Health Check Matrix in alignment with the Tasleemat framework.

docs.title: 1. What?
docs.text: A formal Tasleemat-aligned project artifact known as the Project Health Check Matrix. A structured diagnostic assurance instrument designed to perform an objective evaluation of project vitality across seven core dimensions to safeguard successful delivery.

docs.title: 2. Why?
docs.text: Because without a structured project health check matrix, decisions risk ambiguity and lack objective backing.

docs.title: 3. When?
docs.text: This artifact is prepared during project lifecycle activities and refreshed as required.

docs.title: 4. Who?
docs.text: Responsibilities: Prepared by the designated project lead and approved by key governance authorities.

docs.title: Tailoring Tips
docs.text:
• Scale the depth of analysis to match project complexity and risk.
  • Ensure all key stakeholders are aligned before final sign-off.

docs.title: 1. Pre-requisites & Inputs (Upstream Dependencies)
docs.text:
• Mandatory:
    • Enterprise Strategic Plan
  • Optional / Contextual:
    • Project Charter (PMO-03.01)

docs.title: 2. Downstream Dependents
docs.text:
• Mandatory:
    • Project Governance and Reporting Records

docs.title: 5. How?
docs.text: Fill out each section carefully following the specific field guidance provided below:

docs.title: Review Context
docs.text:
• Review Purpose and Milestone Stage: The objective of the independent health review and the project lifecycle phase or gate at which it is conducted.
  • Lead Reviewer and Assessment Date: The independent PMO auditor or assurance lead conducting the review and the inspection date.
  • Overall Health Rating: The synthesized overall health score (Red, Amber, or Green) representing aggregate delivery confidence.

docs.title: Dimension Health Scores
docs.text:
• Governance and Sponsorship Health: Health rating and findings on steering committee engagement, decision timeliness, and charter mandate.
  • Scope and Change Control Health: Health rating and findings on baseline stability, scope creep control, and change request rigor.
  • Schedule and Milestone Health: Health rating and findings on critical path adherence, milestone float, and delivery velocity.
  • Cost and Budget Variance Health: Health rating and findings on earned value metrics (CPI), cost variance, and EAC forecast credibility.
  • Risk and Issue Exposure Health: Health rating and findings on risk register currency, mitigation effectiveness, and unresolved issues.
  • Stakeholder and Team Health: Health rating and findings on team morale, resourcing levels, and stakeholder satisfaction.

docs.title: Remediation Action Plan
docs.text:
• Critical Finding Description: Key vulnerability or red-flag issue identified during the health check audit.
  • Mandated Corrective Action: Specific remedial intervention required to return the project domain to acceptable performance.
  • Remediation Owner and Due Date: The assigned individual accountable for corrective action execution and the strict due date.

docs.text:
Document Reference: PMO-06.12

This document provides a comprehensive, professional reference to understand the purpose and effective usage of the Flow Metrics and Value Stream Dashboard in alignment with the Tasleemat framework and PMI PMBOK standards.

docs.title: 1. What?
docs.text: A formal Tasleemat-aligned project artifact known as the Flow Metrics and Value Stream Dashboard. A formal modern delivery telemetry instrument tracking Lean/Agile flow metrics (Lead Time, Cycle Time, WIP limits, Flow Efficiency, and Throughput) across product value streams.

docs.title: 2. Why?
docs.text: Because without a structured flow metrics and value stream dashboard, strategic execution risks misalignment, lack of objective telemetry, and compromised governance.

docs.title: 3. When?
docs.text: This artifact is prepared during project lifecycle activities and refreshed across iterative cycles.

docs.title: 4. Who?
docs.text: Responsibilities: Prepared by the designated project lead and approved by accountable governance authorities.

docs.title: Tailoring Tips
docs.text:
• Scale the depth of analysis to match organizational complexity, regulatory standards, and delivery cadence.
  • Ensure all key cross-functional stakeholders are actively engaged throughout lifecycle reviews.

docs.title: 1. Pre-requisites & Inputs (Upstream Dependencies)
docs.text:
• Mandatory:
    • Enterprise Strategic Plan
  • Optional / Contextual:
    • Project Charter (PMO-03.01)

docs.title: 2. Downstream Dependents
docs.text:
• Mandatory:
    • Project Governance and Performance Records

docs.title: 5. How?
docs.text: Fill out each section carefully following the specific field guidance provided below:

docs.title: Value Stream Parameters
docs.text:
• Value Stream Name and Definition: The specific customer value stream, delivery pipeline, or product domain monitored by this flow dashboard.
  • Measurement Window and Interval: The operational reporting period, iteration window, and rolling sample interval evaluated for flow metrics.
  • WIP Limits and Work Categorization: Configured Work in Progress (WIP) caps across workflow stages and item type breakdown (Features, Defect Fixes, Technical Debt, and Risks).

docs.title: Flow Telemetry and Metrics
docs.text:
• Lead Time and Cycle Time Percentiles: 50th, 85th, and 95th percentile delivery times from work commitment to customer deployment, highlighting predictability.
  • Flow Efficiency and Wait Time Ratio: Percentage of total lead time spent in active value-adding touch work versus idle queue/blocking states.
  • Throughput and Delivery Velocity: Completed work items delivered per iteration cycle, indicating steady-state system capacity and throughput stability.

docs.title: Flow Health and Bottleneck Remediation
docs.text:
• Flow Load and Work Age Health: Inventory of active in-flight items, aging WIP items exceeding the 85th percentile threshold, and systemic work overload.
  • Bottleneck Identification and Root Cause: Specific workflow stage where work accumulates as queue inventory and the underlying process constraint.
  • Kaizen Flow Optimization Action: Targeted continuous improvement action, WIP constraint adjustment, or dependency unblocking intervention to improve flow.

docs.text:
Document Reference: PMO-07.01

This document provides a comprehensive, professional reference to understand the purpose and effective usage of the Lessons Learned Summary in alignment with the Tasleemat framework.

docs.title: 1. What?
docs.text: A formal Tasleemat-aligned project document known as the Lessons Learned Summary, used to compile and organize what the project team did that worked very well and should be passed along to other project teams, and to identify what should be improved for future project work. It covers project performance, risks and issues, quality defects, vendor management, areas of exceptional performance, and areas for improvement.

docs.title: 2. Why?
docs.text: To preserve organizational learning so that future projects can adopt what worked and avoid what did not, and to ensure strict alignment with Tasleemat standards.

docs.title: 3. When?
docs.text: This artifact is prepared at the CLOSING Process Group of the project lifecycle: at the close of a phase for long projects, and at the close of the project for shorter projects. It supports process 4.7 Close Project or Phase.

docs.title: 4. Who?
docs.text: Responsibilities: Compiled by the Project Manager with the project team, finalized for sign-off by the Sponsor or Client, and archived in the lessons learned repository alongside the lessons learned register.

docs.title: Tailoring Tips
docs.text:
• Add, combine, or eliminate rows as needed to capture the important aspects of your project.
  • Consider including a section on change management, as that can sometimes be a challenging aspect of projects to manage.
  • You may want to include a section on phase management if you are doing the summary at the end of the project.
  • Integration management is an important aspect for projects that are part of a program or that have multiple organizations working on one project.
  • If your project used a new development approach, such as a blended predictive and adaptive (agile) approach, consider adding some relevant lessons learned.
  • The lessons learned repository can be as simple as a binder, or a searchable database, or anything in between.

docs.text:
• Mandatory:
    • Product Acceptance Form (PMO-06.08)
    • UAT Sign-off (PMO-06.10)
    • Contract Closure Reports (PMO-07.02)
  • Optional / Contextual:

    • Issue Log (PMO-05.01)

docs.title: 2. Downstream Dependents

  • Optional / Contextual:

    • Transition to Operations Checklist (PMO-07.04)

docs.title: 5. How?
docs.text:
To accurately and professionally complete the LESSONS LEARNED SUMMARY, the responsible party must populate the following sections based on the project context (ensure parameters.md is referenced for global project variables):

  • Project Performance / Requirements Definition and Management / What Worked Well: Practices or incidents that were effective in defining and managing requirements. Name the practice, not the meeting where it was discussed.
  • Project Performance / Requirements Definition and Management / What Can Be Improved: Practices or incidents that can be improved in defining and managing requirements, and what the improvement should be.
  • Project Performance / Scope Definition and Management / What Worked Well: Practices or incidents that were effective in defining and managing scope. Where baselines were held, say so.
  • Project Performance / Scope Definition and Management / What Can Be Improved: Practices or incidents that can be improved in defining and managing scope.
  • Project Performance / Schedule Development and Control / What Worked Well: Practices or incidents that were effective in developing and controlling the schedule.
  • Project Performance / Schedule Development and Control / What Can Be Improved: Practices or incidents that can be improved in developing and controlling the schedule.
  • Project Performance / Cost Estimating and Control / What Worked Well: Practices or incidents that were effective in developing estimates and controlling costs.
  • Project Performance / Cost Estimating and Control / What Can Be Improved: Practices or incidents that can be improved in developing estimates and controlling costs.
  • Project Performance / Quality Planning and Control / What Worked Well: Practices or incidents that were effective in planning, managing, and controlling quality.
  • Project Performance / Quality Planning and Control / What Can Be Improved: Practices or incidents that can be improved in planning, managing, and controlling quality. Specific defects are recorded in the quality defects section below.
  • Project Performance / Physical Resource Planning and Control / What Worked Well: Practices or incidents that were effective in planning, acquiring, and managing physical resources.
  • Project Performance / Physical Resource Planning and Control / What Can Be Improved: Practices or incidents that can be improved in planning, acquiring, and managing physical resources.
  • Project Performance / Team Planning, Development, and Performance / What Worked Well: Practices or incidents that were effective in working with team members and developing and managing the team.
  • Project Performance / Team Planning, Development, and Performance / What Can Be Improved: Practices or incidents that can be improved in working with team members and developing and managing the team.
  • Project Performance / Communications Management / What Worked Well: Practices or incidents that were effective in planning and distributing information.
  • Project Performance / Communications Management / What Can Be Improved: Practices or incidents that can be improved in planning and distributing information.
  • Project Performance / Reporting / What Worked Well: Practices or incidents that were effective in reporting project performance.
  • Project Performance / Reporting / What Can Be Improved: Practices or incidents that can be improved in reporting project performance.
  • Project Performance / Risk Management / What Worked Well: Practices or incidents that were effective in the risk management process. Specific risks are recorded in the risks and issues section below.
  • Project Performance / Risk Management / What Can Be Improved: Practices or incidents that can be improved in the risk management process. Specific risks are recorded in the risks and issues section below.
  • Project Performance / Procurement Planning and Management / What Worked Well: Practices or incidents that were effective in planning, conducting, and administering contracts.
  • Project Performance / Procurement Planning and Management / What Can Be Improved: Practices or incidents that can be improved in planning, conducting, and administering contracts.
  • Project Performance / Stakeholder Engagement / What Worked Well: Practices or incidents that were effective in engaging stakeholders.
  • Project Performance / Stakeholder Engagement / What Can Be Improved: Practices or incidents that can be improved in engaging stakeholders.
  • Project Performance / Process Improvement Information / What Worked Well: Processes that were developed and should be continued on future projects.
  • Project Performance / Process Improvement Information / What Can Be Improved: Processes that should be changed or discontinued.
  • Project Performance / Product-Specific Information / What Worked Well: Practices or incidents that were effective in delivering the specific product, service, or result.
  • Project Performance / Product-Specific Information / What Can Be Improved: Practices or incidents that can be improved in delivering the specific product, service, or result.
  • Project Performance / Other / What Worked Well: Other practices or incidents that were effective, such as change control, configuration management, or integration management.
  • Project Performance / Other / What Can Be Improved: Other practices or incidents that can be improved, such as change control, configuration management, or integration management.
  • Risks and Issues / Risk or Issue: Describe the risk or issue that occurred and should be considered to improve organizational learning.
  • Risks and Issues / Response: Describe the response that was taken and its effectiveness. Say plainly whether the response worked.
  • Risks and Issues / Comments: Provide any additional information needed to improve future project performance.
  • Quality Defects / Defect: Describe the quality defect that should be considered to improve organizational effectiveness.
  • Quality Defects / Resolution: Describe how the defect was resolved and whether the resolution held.
  • Quality Defects / Comments: Indicate what should be done to improve future project performance.
  • Vendor Management / Vendor: List the vendor or vendors concerned.
  • Vendor Management / Issue: Describe any issues, claims, or disputes that occurred with this vendor.
  • Vendor Management / Resolution: Describe the outcome or resolution that was reached.
  • Vendor Management / Comments: Indicate what should be done to improve future vendor management performance.
  • Areas of Exceptional Performance / Entry: Identify areas of exceptional performance that can be passed on to other teams. State what was done and what made it work.
  • Areas for Improvement / Entry: Identify areas that can be improved for future performance. State the improvement sought, not only the problem.
