docs.title: Artifact: Contract Closeout Report
docs.text:
Document Reference: PMO-07.02

This document provides a detailed, professional reference for understanding the purpose of the Contract Closeout Report and using it effectively as part of the Tasleemat methodology.

docs.title: 1. What is it?
docs.text: An official Tasleemat document called the Contract Closeout Report, used to document vendor performance so the information can be used to evaluate the vendor for future work. Contract closure supports the project closure process and helps ensure contractual agreements are completed or terminated.

docs.title: 2. Why?
docs.text: To ensure alignment with Tasleemat standards, to provide transparency, to record the lessons learned from a contract for future procurement, and to support project closure.

docs.title: 3. When?
docs.text: This artifact is prepared in the Closing Process Group of the project lifecycle, before a contract can be fully closed or terminated.

docs.title: 4. Who?
docs.text: Responsibilities: Maintained by the contract manager and the procurement manager, and approved by finance control. It is used as an input when the vendor is evaluated for future procurement.

docs.title: Tailoring Tips
docs.text:
• For a small contract you can combine all the vendor performance information into a single summary paragraph.
  • For small contracts you may not need the contract changes or contract disputes sections.
  • If the project was based around one large contract, you can combine the information in the project closeout report with this form.

docs.title: Alignment
docs.text:
• Procurement management plan
  • Procurement audit
  • Change log
  • Project closeout

docs.title: 5. How?
docs.text:
To accurately and professionally complete the CONTRACT CLOSEOUT REPORT, the responsible party must populate the following critical sections based on the project context (ensure parameters.md is referenced for global project variables):

  • Contract Identification: Record the contract reference, the vendor, the contract type and value, and the closeout status.
  • What Worked Well: For scope, quality, schedule, cost, and any other dimension, describe what was handled well and give the evidence for it.
  • What Can Be Improved: For the same five dimensions, describe what could have been improved and the recommended action.
  • Record of Contract Changes: For each change, enter the change ID, the description, and the date approved, taken from the change log.
  • Record of Contract Disputes: For each dispute or claim, describe it, the resolution, and the date it was resolved.
  • Contract Completion and Final Payment: Record the completion date, who signed off, and the date of the final payment.
  • Comments: Add any comments that add relevance to the report.

docs.title: Project Artifact: Project or Phase Closeout
docs.text:
Document Reference: PMO-07.03

This document provides a comprehensive, professional reference to understand the purpose and effective usage of the Project or Phase Closeout in alignment with the Tasleemat framework.

docs.title: 1. What?
docs.text:
A formal Tasleemat-aligned project document known as the Project or Phase Closeout, used to document the final project performance as compared to the project objectives. The objectives from the project charter are reviewed and evidence of meeting them is documented. Where an objective was not met, or where there is a variance, that is documented as well, together with the information from the procurement closeout.

The Performance Summary is a matrix: Scope and Quality as rows, against Objectives, Completion Criteria, and How Met as columns. The Variances section is a second matrix: Time and Cost as rows, against Objectives, Final Outcome, Variance, and Comments.

docs.title: 2. Why?
docs.text: To give the organization a durable record of what the project delivered and what it cost to deliver it, so that decisions about future work rest on evidence rather than recollection, and so that nothing open at closure is silently lost.

docs.title: 3. When?
docs.text: This artifact is prepared at the CLOSING Process Group of the project lifecycle. It supports process 4.7 Close Project or Phase, and is produced at the close of a phase for long projects, and at the close of the project for shorter ones.

docs.title: 4. Who?
docs.text: Responsibilities: Compiled by the Project Manager, signed off by the Project Sponsor or Client and the Operations or Service Owner who receives the product, and archived with the project records.

docs.title: Tailoring Tips
docs.text:
• When working with an incremental life cycle or agile development method, the delivery of a major end item, service, or capability may benefit from a formal phase closeout report.
  • For projects that are part of a program, tailor the content to meet the needs of the program.
  • Add a row to the Performance Summary or the Variances matrix per additional area or measure the project tracks.
  • Use the information from your project to determine the best approach.

docs.title: 1. Pre-requisites & Inputs (Upstream Dependencies)
docs.text:
• Mandatory:
    • Product Acceptance Form (PMO-06.08)
    • UAT Sign-off (PMO-06.10)
    • Contract Closure Reports (PMO-07.02)
  • Optional / Contextual:
    • Lessons Learned Register (PMO-05.07)
    • Issue Log (PMO-05.01)
    • Risk Register (PMO-04.08.02)

docs.title: 2. Downstream Dependents
docs.text:
• Mandatory:
    • Final Project Archive & Release
    • Value Realization Register (PMO-01.03)
    • Organizational Process Assets Update
  • Optional / Contextual:
    • Post-Implementation Review
    • Transition to Operations Checklist (PMO-07.04)

docs.title: 5. How?
docs.text:
To accurately and professionally complete the PROJECT OR PHASE CLOSEOUT, the responsible party must populate the following sections based on the project context (ensure parameters.md is referenced for global project variables):

  • Project Description / Description: Provide a summary-level description of the project or phase: what it was, its purpose, and its boundaries. Keep it to a summary, and point to the project charter for detail.
  • Benefits Management / How Benefits Were Achieved: Describe how the final product, service, or result achieved the benefits the project was undertaken to address. Identify the benefit and the evidence that it was realised, distinguishing a benefit that was realised from one that is still only expected.
  • Benefits Management / Benefits Realisation Status: The current realisation status of each benefit, and who owns tracking it after the project team has been released. A benefit with no owner at closure is a benefit that will not be measured.
  • Business Needs / How Business Needs Were Met: Describe how the final product, service, or result achieved the business needs identified in the business plan.
  • Business Needs / Needs Not Met: Any business need that was not met, and what happens next now that the project is closed. A need left unstated here will be assumed met by whoever inherits the product.
  • Performance Summary / Scope / Objectives: Describe the scope objectives needed to achieve the planned benefits of the project.
  • Performance Summary / Scope / Completion Criteria: Document the specific and measurable criteria needed to complete the scope objectives. State each one so that it can be answered met or not met, and cross-reference the scope baseline.
  • Performance Summary / Scope / How Met: Provide the evidence that the completion criteria were met. Give the source of the evidence, such as the document, test result, or acceptance record, and not only the conclusion drawn from it.
  • Performance Summary / Quality / Objectives: Describe the quality objectives and criteria needed to achieve the planned benefits of the project.
  • Performance Summary / Quality / Completion Criteria: Document the specific and measurable criteria needed to meet the product and project quality objectives.
  • Performance Summary / Quality / How Met: Enter the verification and validation information from the product acceptance form. Cross-reference that form rather than restating it, so the two records cannot drift apart.
  • Variances / Time / Objectives: The planned time objectives: the approved schedule baseline duration and the planned completion date.
  • Variances / Time / Final Outcome: The actual completion date and the actual duration.
  • Variances / Time / Variance: The difference between planned and actual, in days or weeks, with the reason. Where the project finished early, say so and explain why, because an unexplained favourable variance hides a planning error just as a delay does.
  • Variances / Time / Comments: Any consequence of the time variance for the organization, such as a missed market window, and anything still open at closure.
  • Variances / Cost / Objectives: The approved cost baseline, or the total budget at completion if no baseline applies.
  • Variances / Cost / Final Outcome: The actual total spent at completion, stating whether it includes contingency drawn or reserve released.
  • Variances / Cost / Variance: The difference between planned and actual, in currency and as a percentage, with the reason.
  • Variances / Cost / Comments: Any consequence of the cost variance for the organization, such as a claim or a budget transfer still required, and anything still open.
  • Risks and Issues / Risk or Issue: The risk or issue, and where it came from. Give the reference from the risk or issue register rather than restating it.
  • Risks and Issues / Response and Resolution: What was done about it and how effective that was. Say plainly whether it worked.
  • Risks and Issues / Comments: What remains open, and who owns it after closure. An unresolved item transferred without a named recipient has not been transferred.
  • Procurement Closeout / Contracts Closed: The contracts closed out, with the final value and the closure date of each. Where procurement was not used, state that plainly rather than leaving the section blank.
  • Procurement Closeout / Obligations Discharged: The obligations, warranties, and service levels met, transferred, or still outstanding, with the holder named for each.
  • Procurement Closeout / Claims and Disputes Settled: Any claim or dispute settled before closure, and any that was not. An unresolved claim is a liability the project is handing on.

docs.title: Project Artifact: Transition to Operations Checklist
docs.text:
Document Reference: PMO-07.04

This document provides a comprehensive, professional reference to understand the purpose and effective usage of the Transition to Operations Checklist in alignment with the Tasleemat framework.

docs.title: 1. What?
docs.text: A single structured checklist table detailing operational transition items. For every deliverable, system asset, support runbook, and warranty agreement, it records the handover item description, the responsible receiving party, the operational acceptance criteria, the target handover date, and the formal sign-off status.

docs.title: 2. Why?
docs.text: Because successful projects frequently stumble after launch when operations teams are unprepared to maintain new systems. A transition checklist ensures that operational documentation, admin privileges, escalation procedures, and support agreements are formally verified before the project team disbands.

docs.title: 3. When?
docs.text: Initiated during the closing phase (or during phased delivery cutovers), maintained throughout the hypercare and transition window, and finalized upon obtaining formal operational acceptance prior to project closeout.

docs.title: 4. Who?
docs.text: Jointly executed by the Project Manager and the receiving Operations / Service Owner, with verification by the Client Representative. All three sign off to confirm that operational readiness requirements have been fully satisfied.

docs.title: Tailoring Tips
docs.text:
• Involve operations early. Engage operational stakeholders during testing and dry runs, not only at final handover.
  • Verify documentation and access. Ensure runbooks, user manuals, administrative credentials, and licensing agreements are verified and archived.
  • Establish warranty and escalation paths. Clarify the warranty support window and transition from hypercare to standard tier-1/tier-2 support.
  • Sign off each item individually. Avoid blanket acceptances that obscure unfulfilled operational prerequisites.

docs.title: 1. Pre-requisites & Inputs (Upstream Dependencies)
docs.text:
• Mandatory:

    • UAT Sign-off (PMO-06.10)
    • Contract Closure Reports (PMO-07.02)
  • Optional / Contextual:
    • Lessons Learned Register (PMO-05.07)
    • Issue Log (PMO-05.01)
    • Risk Register (PMO-04.08.02)

docs.title: 2. Downstream Dependents
docs.text:
• Mandatory:
    • Final Project Archive & Release
    • Value Realization Register (PMO-01.03)
    • Organizational Process Assets Update
  • Optional / Contextual:
    • Post-Implementation Review
    • Transition to Operations Checklist (PMO-07.04)

docs.title: 5. How?
docs.text:
To accurately complete the Transition to Operations Checklist, populate the following sections based on the project context (ensuring reference to parameters.md for the general project variables):

  • Handover Item: The operational deliverable, documentation, system asset, credentials, warranty, or support agreement formally transferred to the sustaining operations team.
  • Responsible Party: The operational team, service owner, or designated role accepting ongoing responsibility and stewardship for the item.
  • Acceptance Criteria: The specific operational readiness criteria and verification evidence required before formal handover sign-off.
  • Handover Date: The scheduled or actual date on which ownership and support accountability are formally transferred.
  • Sign-off Status: The formal verification status (e.g., Accepted, Conditional, Pending) confirming operational readiness.

docs.title: Project Artifact: Post-Implementation Review Report
docs.text:
Document Reference: PMO-07.05

This document provides a comprehensive, professional reference to understand the purpose and effective usage of the Post-Implementation Review Report in alignment with the Tasleemat framework.

docs.title: 1. What?
docs.text: A formal Tasleemat-aligned project artifact known as the Post-Implementation Review Report. A formal closing and benefits realization audit document conducted 3 to 6 months after project handover to assess sustained value realization, operational adoption, and long-term organizational impacts.

docs.title: 2. Why?
docs.text: Because without a structured post-implementation review report, decisions risk ambiguity and lack objective backing.

docs.title: 3. When?
docs.text: This artifact is prepared during project lifecycle activities and refreshed as required.

docs.title: 4. Who?
docs.text: Responsibilities: Prepared by the designated project lead and approved by key governance authorities.

docs.title: Tailoring Tips
docs.text:
• Scale the depth of analysis to match project complexity and risk.
  • Ensure all key stakeholders are aligned before final sign-off.

docs.title: 1. Pre-requisites & Inputs (Upstream Dependencies)
docs.text:
• Mandatory:
    • Enterprise Strategic Plan
  • Optional / Contextual:
    • Project Charter (PMO-03.01)

docs.title: 2. Downstream Dependents
docs.text:
• Mandatory:
    • Project Governance and Reporting Records

docs.title: 5. How?
docs.text: Fill out each section carefully following the specific field guidance provided below:

docs.title: Review Context
docs.text:
• Review Purpose and Evaluation Period: The post-handover evaluation objectives and the operating timeframe assessed (typically 3 to 6 months post go-live).
  • Lead Evaluator and Date: The designated business assurance lead or PMO evaluator conducting the review and the completion date.

docs.title: Benefits Realization Assessment
docs.text:
• Planned vs Realized Benefits: Quantitative comparison of financial and operational benefits realized in steady-state operations versus business case projections.
  • Operational Adoption Rate: Metrics reflecting user adoption, system throughput, and behavioral integration into routine operations.

docs.title: Operational Transition and Stability
docs.text:
• Operational Stability and Support: Assessment of post-transition SLA adherence, support ticket volume, and operational maintenance handover efficacy.
  • Outstanding Issues and Technical Debt: Inventory of lingering operational bugs, unresolved defects, or technical debt requiring long-term maintenance.

docs.title: Long-Term Insights and Recommendations
docs.text:
• Strategic Lessons Learned: High-level strategic insights on solution viability, change management effectiveness, and business model impact.
  • Ongoing Optimization Recommendations: Prescriptive guidance for continuous optimization, future phase enhancements, and long-term capability extension.
